title: Celebration of Life Planning Checklist
subtitle: A gentle guide for gathering family and friends to honor someone you love
intro: Planning a celebration of life is hard, and you do not have to do it perfectly or all at once. This checklist breaks it into small steps and gives you places to write things down, so you can share the work with people who want to help. Take what is useful and leave the rest.

sections.heading: The First Days
sections.note: There is no right order. Do what you can, and ask for help with the rest.

groups.title: Right away
items: Choose one or two people to be the main contacts for family and vendors.
Gather important documents such as the will, insurance papers, and any written wishes.
Ask whether your loved one left wishes for a service, burial, or cremation.
Contact the funeral home or cremation provider if you are working with one.
Decide on a date range for the gathering, allowing time for out-of-town family.
Write down what you decide so you do not have to repeat it.
Decide whether the gathering will be private, open to all, or invitation only.
Ask the family which religious or cultural customs they would like included.
Check on any wishes about flowers, music, or readings.

groups.title: Telling people
items: Make a short list of the people who should hear first.
Ask a trusted friend or relative to help spread the word.
Write a brief message with the date, time, and place once they are set.
Share the request for flowers, donations, or no gifts, if you have one.
Post a notice if you wish, and ask a helper to manage replies.
Consider a short phone tree so no one has to make every call.
Let work, school, and community groups know.

groups.title: Take care of yourself
items: Eat something and drink water.
Accept offers of meals, rides, and childcare.
Assign a helper to answer calls and messages.
Plan a quiet moment before the gathering.
Remember that there is no single right way to grieve.

sections.heading: Planning Timeline
sections.note: Celebrations of life are often held within one to four weeks, but timing is up to your family.

tasks: Choose a date range and gather the immediate family to decide on the style of gathering.
Contact potential venues and ask about availability.
Ask a few helpers to take on specific roles.
Confirm the plan for burial, cremation, or memorial.
Book the venue and confirm the time, length, and setup rules.
Choose the officiant, celebrant, or family member who will lead.
Order food or arrange for family and friends to contribute.
Reserve tables, chairs, linens, and any needed tent.
Send word to guests with a simple message.
Check parking, ramps, and seating for guests with mobility needs.
Plan an alternate if the weather affects an outdoor space.
Finalize the program and who will speak.
Gather photos and keepsakes for display.
Arrange music, a slideshow, or a playlist.
Confirm the final headcount with the venue and food provider.
Plan parking and accessibility for older guests.
Confirm delivery and setup times for rentals.
Print programs, photos, or memory cards.
Set up the memory table or display if you have access to the venue.
Share the schedule with helpers.
Pack tissues, water, and a small emergency kit.
Confirm who is bringing food and where it will be stored.
Charge phones, speakers, and the slideshow device.
Arrive early and walk the space with a helper.
Assign a greeter at the door and someone to manage the guest book.
Keep the schedule flexible and give speakers extra time.
Have someone check on older guests and young children.
Plan a quiet space for family to step away.
Collect flowers, photos, and keepsakes.
Return rentals and clean the venue.
Send thank-you notes when you feel ready.
Share photos and the program with those who could not attend.

sections.heading: Venue Options
sections.note: The right place is one that feels comfortable to your family and fits your guests.
rows: Small, informal gatherings; a familiar and personal setting
Parking, restrooms, space, weather plan, chairs and tables
Place of worship or community hall
Simple food service and easy cleanup
Funeral home chapel or reception room

sections.heading: Program and Order of Service
sections.note: A short program is often enough. Most gatherings run 60 to 90 minutes before food and mingling.

groups.title: Opening
items: Welcome from a family member or celebrant.
Music as guests arrive.
A moment of silence or a short reading.
Brief explanation of the plan for the gathering.
Ask a helper to hand out programs and tissues as guests arrive.

groups.title: Remembering
items: Two or three prepared speakers.
Open-mic time for guests to share a short memory.
A slideshow or video with favorite photos.
A favorite poem, song, or passage.
A tribute from children or grandchildren.
Give speakers a gentle time limit of three to five minutes.
Ask speakers to send a copy of their words to a helper in case they need someone to read them aloud.

groups.title: Closing
items: Closing words or a blessing.
A favorite song or a group toast.
Invitation to share food and stories.
Notes on where to find the memory table and guest book.
Plan how guests will leave, such as a recessional song or a quiet exit.

groups.title: At the venue
items: A greeter at the door to help people feel welcome.
Extra chairs near the back for people who arrive late.
A quiet room or corner for family.
Water and tissues in several spots.
Clear signs for restrooms, food, and the memory table.
A place for coats, umbrellas, and winter boots in cold or wet weather.

groups.title: Rentals and supplies
items: Chairs sized to the number of people seated for the program.
Tables for food, the memory table, and the guest book.
Linens in calm colors.
Serving equipment such as chafing dishes and coffee urns.
Plates, cups, and utensils, or a rental set for easier cleanup.
A tent or canopy if the gathering is outdoors.

sections.heading: Memory Table Ideas
sections.note: A memory table helps guests connect with the person you are honoring. Choose a few items, not everything.
rows: Gives the room a focal point
Choose a recent and happy photo
Tells their story over the years
Keep them sturdy and easy to handle
Print copies for guests to take
Provide pens and a sturdy box
Use battery-operated candles if the venue prefers
Brings their taste into the room

sections.heading: Repast Food Amounts
sections.note: Rough guidelines for a meal or reception after the service. Families often bring dishes, so adjust as needed.

sections.heading: Who Does What
sections.note: People often say, "Let me know what I can do." This table lets you answer them.
rows: Greet guests and manage the guest book

sections.heading: Budget Split
sections.note: Rough shares to help you think through costs. Many families spend much less, and that is perfectly fine.

lines.tip: Potluck contributions from family and friends can reduce this a lot.
Community rooms and parks often cost less than event spaces.
Only rent what you need for the number of guests who will be there at once.
A few meaningful arrangements are enough.
A simple one-page program works well.
A speaker and a playlist can work for small gatherings.
Ask about fees or donations in advance.
Set aside a small cushion for unexpected needs.

sections.heading: Gathering Worksheet
sections.note: Write things down here so you do not have to hold them in your head.
fields: Name of the person being honored
